transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-04 15:00 PST
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Alex Ruiz (Redwood Solutions), Priya Shah (NexaRetail CTO), Ben Ortiz (Nexa SRE), Hannah Lee (Nexa ML Eng), Omar Velasquez (Nexa Product)

--- Optional auto-generated summary (may be imperfect) ---
Maya: Quick recap we wanted to focus on throughput tuning — continuous batching and scheduler knobs, make sure the KV cache and token limits won't blow latency SLOs, and talk quantization for cost.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining... um I think we have about an hour, so we'll jump straight in. Liam will lead technical bits. Priya, thanks for making time.
[00:26] Priya: Thanks, Maya. Quick context — we're running two models in prod, one 8B for chat and a smaller 3B for classification. Peak QPS is ~120 req/s, p95 latency target is 300ms for chat, but cost is ballooning. We're trying to see where to tune.
[00:48] Liam: Cool, thanks. Can you confirm deployment mode — hosted or VPC?
[00:56] Ben: We're on Redwood Dedicated now, but plan a VPC/private deployment in Q1. Need to understand what changes when we move to on-prem.
[01:12] Liam: Got it. We'll cover both. First, continuous batching behavior — it's our main knob for throughput. It groups inflight requests but we have to tune the max_num_seqs and token caps.
[01:30] Hannah: Quick question, does continuous batching increase latency variance? We can't have long tail spikes.
[01:42] Liam: It can if the batching window grows to wait for more seqs. We have a scheduler that balances throughput vs latency via two settings: max_num_seqs and the batching timeout. If you set max_num_seqs high, throughput improves but p95 can worsen unless you limit per-request token limits.
[02:05] Priya: What's reasonable for max_num_seqs on A100-ish hardware?
[02:12] Liam: For your 8B model, we typically see sweet spot around 12-20 sequences on A100 80GB with optimized kernels, but it depends on sequence lengths. For many short seqs (<=64 tokens) push higher; for long sequences (>512) keep it lower.
[02:35] Ben: Our typical chat messages are 40–120 tokens. History sometimes adds 200 tokens.
[02:45] Liam: If history is common, recommend ceiling the history length server-side or use prefix caching — that's where KV cache saves you.
[02:56] Maya: Quick note, we sometimes see the product call it K V cash in transcripts — sorry auto captions. but it's KV cache.
[03:06] Hannah: How does KV cache interplay with batching? If we cache prefixes, does that reduce token compute in batch?
[03:17] Liam: Yes, prefix/KV caching reduces repeated compute by reusing key-value states for common prefixes. In continuous batching, cached prefixes are applied and only new tokens are processed. That reduces per-request token count which improves throughput and reduces batch compute time. However, mixing cached and uncached requests in the same batch can complicate scheduling — we tag requests by cache-key and try to batch compatible ones.
[03:43] Priya: Does that mean we should shard traffic by conversation length or cache-hit probability?
[03:52] Liam: Ideally yes. You can route high cache-hit traffic to a fast path with bigger batches and route cold traffic to smaller batches or fallback models.
[04:05] Omar: Is that routing automatic in Redwood or do we need custom logic?
[04:11] Alex: Redwood's smart routing can do policy-based routing — e.g., by header or tag. But for fine-grained routing by cache-hit it's often simplest to add a lightweight tag from the app that indicates a cache hit or estimated token-length.
[04:29] Priya: Ok. Back to scheduler knobs — what are the exact parameters we should tune?
[04:35] Liam: Main ones: max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), batch_timeout_ms, max_tokens_per_batch, and per-request token cap. There are also autoscaling burst knobs but that's more infra.
[04:48] Ben: For batch_timeout_ms, how low do we set it before throughput collapses?
[04:54] Liam: It's workload dependent. For chat with 120 QPS, a short timeout like 10–20ms with max_num_seqs around 12 often hits throughput without adding too much latency. If you set timeout too low you lose batching efficiency. We usually test with a sweep: batch_timeout = [10,20,50,100], max_num_seqs = [8,12,20].
[05:18] Hannah: Can Redwood share a sample sweep config?
[05:21] Maya: Yes — Action item: we'll send YAML with suggested ranges.
[05:28] Priya: How do token limits factor in? If we cap per-request tokens to 256, will that drop quality for long-history context?
[05:38] Liam: There's tradeoff. Capping tokens reduces worst-case compute and keeps batch sizes predictable. For long-history, consider truncated context + retrieval or on-the-fly compression. Also client-side history trimming with key turns works well. For quality, you can keep last N messages and store summaries for older context.
[05:58] Ben: About quantization — we saw 8-bit asymmetric and some int4 papers. What's practical?
[06:06] Liam: For production ondedicated GPUs, 8-bit quantization (e.g., GPTQ/LLM.int8) gives safe latency/cost improvements with minimal quality loss on many models. int4 and aggressive quantization is possible but more risk — we recommend validating on your eval set. Also quantization affects kernel selection — some runtimes will fall back to slower kernels for unsupported quant types.
[06:33] Priya: If quantization changes kernels, could that hurt latency even if compute reduces?
[06:39] Liam: Yes, sometimes quantized models use different CUDA kernels or fused ops. You might see lower compute but worse memory access patterns causing modest latency increase. That’s why we benchmark both latency and throughput — not just FLOPs.
[06:57] Hannah: Do we support mixed precision per-layer?
[07:01] Liam: We can do layer-wise quantization profiles. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles based on your evals. I'll follow up with recommended profiles for your two models.
[07:12] Omar: On VPC/on-prem — we have constrained networking and limited GPU count at first. How much of the tuning is different off-hosted?
[07:23] Alex: The runtime is the same, but autoscaling and cross-region fallback differ. On-prem you'll want stricter batch targets and maybe more aggressive cache strategies to reduce network-bound calls. Also pre-warming and reserved kernel cache matters more with cold starts.
[07:41] Ben: Any gotchas for private deployment regarding KV cache storage?
[07:47] Liam: KV cache can be in-memory per-GPU, or sharded across nodes if you enable distributed KV. On private infra, ensure GPU memory headroom for cache. If you have heavy long-history sessions, KV cache can blow memory. We usually set per-session cache caps and eviction policies.
[08:08] Priya: Can we evict old conversation keys automatically?
[08:12] Liam: Yes — LRU-based eviction or time-based TTLs are typical. We'll share default policies.
[08:19] Maya: Running through a quick example: assume 120 QPS with 80% short messages (~60 tokens) and 20% long (~300 tokens). With max_num_seqs 16 and timeout 20ms, what throughput change would you expect?
[08:36] Liam: Rough rule: batching short messages gives near linear speedups per GPU until memory/compute saturates. You might see 2–3x throughput improvement on the short-path versus no batching. Mixed workloads reduce effective speedup; if long messages dominate you see less. We'll model this in the sample spreadsheet.
[08:58] Priya: Please share that spreadsheet.
[09:01] Maya: Will do. Also, we'll include estimated token-unit cost changes for quantization.
[09:08] Omar: How do we measure good p95 vs cost? Is there an internal metric?
[09:13] Alex: We use p95 latency under production QPS with the same traffic mix, plus cost per 1M tokens. Redwood Console breaks down token-level cost and latency per route. For SLOs, run bench with slightly higher than target QPS to see headroom.
[09:31] Ben: If we need to lower p95 but keep cost low, what's the priority? dedicated hardware or model size reduction?
[09:39] Liam: Order: batching & cache optimizations first, quantization second, then model distillation or smaller model variants, and finally reserved hardware or higher tier GPUs. Routing to smaller models for low-criticality responses is also effective.
[09:54] Hannah: Any quick wins for us right now?
[09:58] Liam: Three quick wins: 1) enforce per-request token cap (e.g., 256) and summary older context, 2) enable prefix KV cache for common prompts, 3) sweep max_num_seqs with batch_timeout small several steps.
[10:14] Priya: Sounds good. On autoscaling knobs — we saw transient queue spikes in the last incident. How do we keep queues from growing?
[10:23] Liam: Use two-tier autoscaling: fast burst pool + normal pool. Fast pool takes brief spikes and has pre-warmed instances. Also set a max concurrency per-instance to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[10:37] Ben: Do you have recommended pre-warm counts?
[10:40] Liam: Depends on traffic CV. For your profile I'd recommend enough to cover 10–15% of peak QPS as pre-warm. We'll include formulas.
[10:52] Omar: There's mention of scheduler fairness — can batching starve low-latency requests?
[10:58] Liam: Could happen. We support priority lanes — low-latency lane with small batches and higher cost, and best-effort lane that batches aggressively. Tagging requests and routing accordingly is key.
[11:15] Priya: How are we doing on observability? We need per-route per-model p95 by region.
[11:22] Maya: Redwood Console already provides per-route dashboards; we can add an alert for p95 breach and token cost anomalies.
[11:30] Hannah: For quantization validation — should we do A/B tests?
[11:35] Liam: Yes, run canary with subset traffic and track eval metrics and user metrics. Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback.
[11:46] Priya: Regarding tokenization differences — we had a case where token counts changed after model update and batching shifted. Any advice?
[11:55] Liam: Always baseline token distribution per model version in your eval harness. The batching strategy should use those distributions. If tokenization increases, re-run the sweep.
[12:07] Ben: On the implementation side, where do we set max_num_seqs — at request router or per-model config?
[12:13] Liam: Per-model config is typical, exposed as model_profile in Redwood Dedicated. You can also override per-route.
[12:22] Priya: If we make very aggressive max_num_seqs, is there an upper safety cap?
[12:27] Liam: Yes, the runtime enforces a hard cap to prevent OOM; we set soft limits by default. We'll share your tenant's current caps.
[12:37] Hannah: Is there any difference in behavior between GPU types (A100 vs H100) for batching?
[12:43] Liam: H100 has better sparsity and throughput for certain kernels; often you can push higher max_num_seqs. But memory footprint and kernel maturity matters. We'll include recommended starting points per GPU family.
[12:58] Maya: Let's talk about token limits again — we can implement a server-side token clamp that returns a 4xx or truncates. Which do customers prefer?
[13:06] Priya: We prefer graceful truncation with a warning header so client can decide. 4xx breaks UX.
[13:12] Ben: Agreed. Truncate + return header like X-Redwood-Truncated: true.
[13:19] Liam: Good plan — we'll provide config snippet.
[13:24] Omar: Any caveats with continuous batching and function calling / streaming?
[13:31] Liam: Streaming can be trickier because you want low latency first tokens. For streaming we use small batch lanes or immediate flush for first token then batch the rest where possible. Function calling is fine but ensure your inferencer can support streaming flush semantics.
[13:52] Priya: We use function calling for structured outputs a lot. Will batching change function call latency?
[13:59] Liam: Slightly — if you put function calls on low-latency lane it should be negligible. Otherwise batch can add a small delay.
[14:08] Maya: I'm going to share a short checklist: sample sweep YAML, scheduler doc, cache eviction defaults, quantization guidance, and sample console queries.
[14:18] Priya: Great. Anything else on on-prem network constraints?
[14:23] Liam: Keep model weights local — avoid NFS for active models; use local SSDs and prefetch weights during pre-warm. Network-bound KV lookups should be cached locally or use memcached tier.
[14:37] Ben: For our staging run, should we test for both cache-hot and cache-cold mixes?
[14:43] Hannah: Yes, we'll create scenarios: 80/20 hot/cold and 50/50.
[14:49] Liam: Perfect. Include spike scenarios.
[14:53] Priya: Any recommended logging levels for perf traces?
[14:58] Alex: Trace-level for a sampling (~1%) and info-level for all requests. The trace payloads help identify batching composition.
[15:08] Maya: Ok we'll capture traces for the stress run.
[15:12] [pause, small cross-talk]
[15:30] Priya: Quick note — legal asked about SOC2 and storage of KV cache. Is that covered?
[15:36] Maya: Yes we encrypt KV in transit and at rest when using managed services; in private you control KMS. We'll send compliance pack.
[15:47] Ben: Let's close with explicit next steps and owners.
[15:52] Maya: Sure — recap: Redwood sends scheduler doc, YAML sweep, quantization guidance, and sample spreadsheet. Nexa runs stress tests and uploads logs; then we review.
[16:06] Priya: Sounds good.
[16:10] Omar: One last thing — can we get a quick expected cost delta for 8-bit quantization? Even a ballpark helps.
[16:17] Liam: Usually 20–40% token-unit cost reduction, depending on model and kernel efficiency. We'll include ranges in the spreadsheet.
[16:27] Hannah: Thanks, everyone.
[16:29] Maya: Thanks, will follow up via email with artifacts.
